SCOPE: this is a note on SIMPLE distillation and it is written as a complete answer on that one method — principle, apparatus, procedure, worked example and uses. It does not survey the whole distillation family; the modified forms are named in the last step only where they mark the limit of this method. APPARATUS IN WORDS, NOT A FIGURE: the flask with a side arm, the thermometer bulb level with the opening of the side arm, the water condenser and the receiver are described precisely enough to be drawn from the words. BOILING POINTS USED: chloroform 334 K and aniline 457 K, a gap of 123 K. A difference of 40 K and a difference of 40 °C are the same difference, since the kelvin and the degree Celsius are equal in size, so the 40 °C rule of thumb is quoted as 40 K where the example is in kelvin.

steps.label: What distillation is used for
lines: Distillation purifies a liquid by
boiling it and condensing the vapour
back to a liquid in a separate vessel.
It is used in two cases.
First, for a volatile liquid mixed with
a non-volatile impurity.
Second, for a mixture of two liquids
whose boiling points differ by more than
about 40 °C.
steps.why: Distillation separates on one property only, volatility, so it is worth stating at the start exactly when that property differs enough to be useful. Below a gap of about 40 °C the vapour that comes off is still a mixture and a single distillation does not purify anything.
common_mistakes: Saying distillation separates any mixture of liquids. The boiling points must differ by more than about 40 °C.
Leaving out the non-volatile impurity case. It is the commoner of the two in the laboratory.
steps.memory_tip: Two cases: a non-volatile impurity, or a boiling point gap wider than about 40 °C.
steps.margin_note: Open with both cases and give the 40 °C figure as a number, not as "a big difference".

steps.label: The principle
steps.mark_note: Vapour pressure and the richer vapour
lines: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure
becomes equal to the pressure above it,
which in an ordinary distillation is the
pressure of the atmosphere.
At any one temperature the liquid with
the lower boiling point has the higher
vapour pressure, so it vaporises more
readily.
The vapour rising from the mixture is
therefore richer in the more volatile
liquid than the mixture in the flask is.
That vapour is led away and condensed in
a different vessel, so the two liquids
end up in two places.
A non-volatile impurity has almost no
vapour pressure of its own, so none of
it passes into the vapour at all and it
stays in the flask.
steps.why: The separation is not caused by the boiling point on its own but by the vapour pressure at the temperature the flask is actually at. The liquid with the lower boiling point has the higher vapour pressure at every temperature, and that is why it is always the one that comes over first.
common_mistakes: Saying the lower boiling liquid boils and the other does not. Both contribute vapour; the vapour is simply much richer in the more volatile one.
Saying the vapour that comes over is pure. From a mixture of two liquids it is richer, not pure, which is why the first fraction is redistilled if very high purity is wanted.
steps.memory_tip: Boiling is vapour pressure equalling the pressure above the liquid, and the more volatile liquid always has the higher vapour pressure.
steps.margin_note: Two marks here, so give the vapour pressure definition of boiling AND the reason the vapour is richer in one liquid.

steps.label: The apparatus
lines: The liquid is placed in a
round-bottomed distillation flask fitted
with a side arm.
A thermometer is fixed through the neck
with its bulb just level with the
opening of the side arm, so that it
reads the temperature of the vapour and
not of the boiling liquid.
The side arm is joined to a water
condenser, a long inner tube surrounded
by a jacket through which cold water is
passed.
The far end of the condenser leads into
a receiver.
A few pieces of porcelain are dropped
into the flask to keep the boiling
smooth.
steps.why: The position of the thermometer bulb is the one detail that decides whether the reading means anything. Level with the side arm it reads the vapour that is actually leaving, which is the temperature that identifies the fraction being collected.
common_mistakes: Dipping the thermometer bulb into the liquid. It is set level with the opening of the side arm, so that it reads the vapour.
Passing the cooling water in at the top of the condenser. It enters at the lower end and leaves at the upper, so the jacket stays full.
steps.memory_tip: Flask with a side arm, thermometer bulb level with that side arm, water condenser, receiver.
steps.margin_note: Describe the apparatus part by part in words, and be exact about where the thermometer bulb sits.

steps.label: The procedure
lines: The flask is heated slowly and evenly.
The thermometer reading rises and then
stays steady while the more volatile
liquid distils over.
The distillate collected while the
reading is steady is that liquid, and it
is kept as the first fraction.
When that liquid is used up the reading
rises again, so the receiver is changed
and the small quantity that comes over
during the rise is set aside.
The reading then steadies at the boiling
point of the second liquid, and a second
fraction is collected in a fresh
receiver.
A non-volatile impurity does not distil
at all and is left in the flask as the
residue.
steps.why: A steady thermometer reading is the signal that only one liquid is passing over, so the collecting vessel is changed at every rise and never in the middle of a steady stretch. That is how the distillate is divided into fractions that are each one substance.
common_mistakes: Collecting everything in one receiver. The receiver is changed each time the thermometer reading rises.
Heating fast. A fast boil carries mixed vapour over and the reading never steadies.
steps.memory_tip: A steady reading means one liquid is coming over; a rising reading means it is time to change the receiver.
steps.margin_note: Two marks here, so write the whole run: the steady reading, the change of receiver, and the residue left behind.

steps.label: A worked example
lines: A mixture of chloroform and aniline is
separated by simple distillation.
Chloroform boils at 334 K and aniline
boils at 457 K.
The gap is 123 K, much wider than the
difference of about 40 K that this
method needs.
Chloroform distils over first and is
collected, and aniline is left in the
flask until the temperature is raised
to 457 K.
steps.why: A worked example turns the rule into a number. The gap of 123 K is three times the minimum, so the vapour coming off at 334 K is chloroform with almost no aniline in it, and one distillation is enough.
common_mistakes: Giving aniline as the first distillate. Chloroform has the lower boiling point, 334 K against 457 K.
Quoting the boiling points without saying what the gap is. The size of the gap is what justifies the method.
steps.memory_tip: Chloroform 334 K, aniline 457 K: a gap of 123 K, far more than the 40 K a simple distillation needs.
steps.margin_note: Write both boiling points and subtract them on the page. The number 123 K is the justification.

steps.label: Uses and where the method stops
lines: Distillation is used to purify solvents,
to separate a liquid product from a
reaction mixture, and to recover a
solvent after an extraction.
It has two limits.
It cannot separate two liquids whose
boiling points are close together, and a
fractionating column is needed for that.
It cannot be used for a liquid that
decomposes below its boiling point, and
the pressure has to be lowered for that.

lines.text: The more volatile liquid distils first

steps.why: Naming the two limits is what makes the note complete: they are exactly the two situations that the modified forms of distillation were devised for, so stating them shows where simple distillation ends and why anything else is needed.
common_mistakes: Ending at the procedure. A note on a method should say what it is used for and where it stops working.
Saying distillation works for every liquid. A liquid that decomposes before it boils cannot be distilled at ordinary pressure.
steps.memory_tip: Two limits: boiling points too close, or a liquid that decomposes before it boils.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming which liquid comes over first completes the answer.

insider_note: A note on simple distillation, so build it in six parts: the two cases, the vapour pressure principle, the apparatus with the thermometer bulb level with the side arm, the run with its steady readings and changed receivers, a named example with both boiling points, and the uses with the two limits. Chloroform at 334 K and aniline at 457 K give a gap of 123 K, and that number is the justification for the method. The sixth part is the one most answers leave out: distillation purifies solvents and separates a liquid product from a reaction mixture, and it stops at two things — boiling points too close together, and a liquid that decomposes before it boils.
